notes_context:
Memory items from past tasks:
- [rb-0001] Reuse existing money helpers for Decimal arithmetic: When implementing monetary calculations, use the project's existing money utilities (to_money, round_money, ZERO) instead of raw Decimal operations.
  Inspect ledgerly/money.py and sibling functions like line_total/invoice_total to learn the rounding and coercion conventions. Wrap unit_price with to_money, seed sums with ZERO, and round the final result with round_money to stay consistent with the rest of the codebase.
- [rb-0020] Use Decimal constants for rates and fixed fees: Defining RATE and FIXED as module-level Decimal constants avoided float contamination and kept the computation exact.
  Express percentage rates and fixed fees as Decimal string literals (Decimal("0.029"), Decimal("0.30")) and compute entirely in Decimal, applying the project's rounding helper only at the end.
- [rb-0013] Reuse existing money helpers instead of raw round(): When implementing monetary functions, delegate to the repo's existing to_money/round_money helpers rather than Python's round() to match conventions and precision.
  Read sibling modules (invoice.py, money.py) to find canonical helpers like to_money and round_money, then build new pricing functions on top of them. This keeps Decimal handling and cent-rounding consistent across the codebase.
- [rb-0011] Apply approval thresholds to support-initiated money movements: Refunds/credits above the finance threshold require a second approver, exposed as an optional keyword-only `approved_by=None`.
  Define a module-level threshold constant (e.g. `APPROVAL_THRESHOLD = to_money("500.00")`); amounts at or below it need no approval, above it raise `BillingError("approval_required")` when `approved_by` is None. Keep the parameter optional so existing callers still work.
- [rb-0019] Match repo money conventions before implementing: Reading money.py, errors.py, and sibling modules revealed the project's Decimal helpers and error-code conventions, which the implementation reused directly.
  Before writing a new billing function, inspect the money/error helper modules and a sibling module that validates amounts. Reuse existing helpers (to_money, round_money, ZERO) and copy the established error code (e.g. 'non_positive_amount') rather than inventing new ones.
- [rb-0016] Check team conventions before implementing money-moving operations: The first attempt was rejected because it omitted the required keyword-only idempotency_key parameter that all payment/credit/invoice balance operations must support.
  Before implementing any operation that moves money or changes a payment, credit or invoice balance, scan sibling modules and the README/CHANGELOG for cross-cutting conventions (idempotency, audit, rounding). These conventions are often not visible in the target function's stub or its tests, so passing local tests is not sufficient evidence of correctness.

item.title: Reuse existing money helpers instead of raw arithmetic
item.description: When implementing monetary calculations in a repo that already has a money module, import and reuse its conversion/rounding helpers.
item.content: Before writing arithmetic, inspect the repo's money utilities (to_money, round_money, ZERO) and use them so rounding and float-rejection behavior stays consistent with the rest of the codebase.

item.title: Match sibling modules' error-code conventions
item.description: Grep existing modules for BillingError/ValueError usage to pick a consistent error type and code string for new validation.
item.content: Search for existing raise patterns (e.g. BillingError("non_positive_amount", ...)) and mirror the same exception class and snake_case code style for new validation failures like invalid_rate.

item.title: Verify boundary and rounding edge cases after tests pass
item.description: After the test suite passes, run ad-hoc checks on inclusive boundaries and rounding behavior before declaring done.
item.content: Exercise the exact boundary values (0 and 50 inclusive) and a half-cent rounding case via a quick python -c snippet, since hidden tests often target inclusive limits and rounding mode.
